A customer's question

"Do these water filters leak?"

You have 30,000 reviews and a search box. What should it return?

Search problem!

A search box doesn't read questions; it matches words. "Do these water filters leak?" becomes water filter leak, and since every review below is about a water filter, the word that decides is leak. 3 minutes: which of these reviews should come back?

  1. "Started leaking after 2 weeks."
  2. "No leaks at all, great filter."
  3. "The leakproof lid is great."
  1. "LEAKED within a day. Returning it."
  2. "Water dripped all over the floor."
  3. "My old filter leaked, this one is perfect."

First say the bridge out loud: the customer asked a question, but the search box only sees the words in it. In a Boolean engine, turning a question into keywords is the customer's job, and it stays that way until the later workshops. Then give everyone 3 minutes, then take a vote on each. The point is that "should it match" has two layers: does the word match (1, 4, 6 yes, 3 no, 5 no), and is the review a leak complaint (1, 4 yes; 2, 3, 6 no; 5 yes but no shared word). Today we fix the first layer. The second needs the later workshops.

Different approaches of search

Search Reviews What goes wrong
the string leak, any case 924 also orleaks, groundsleaked, leakproof
the exact word leak 314 misses Leaks, leaking, leaked
every form of leak: leak, leaks, leaked, leaking, any case 885 but 408 of them say no leaks, won't leak, …

Today we fix the first two rows: decide what counts as a word, and which words count as the same. The third row, telling "it leaks" from "it doesn't leak", needs the later workshops.

"Every form" means every word a stemmer reduces to leak: in these reviews that is exactly leak, leaks, leaked and leaking. Stemming is how we get there; it comes later today. Leakage and leaky are not included: the Porter stemmer turns them into leakag and leaki.

That's what a search engine does

Text"It LEAKED again, still leaking!"
→
Tokensit · leaked · again · still · leaking
tokenise
→
Termsit · leak · again · still · leak
normalise
→
Indexleak → 28, 40, 94, …
invert
→
Answersleak AND NOT coffee
query

A token is a word exactly as it appears in the text: leaked and leaking are two different tokens. A term is what is left after normalising, the form the index stores and the query looks up: both become the term leak.

First half: tokens and terms (W02-A). Second half: the index and the queries (W02-B).

Concept + hand calculation

Tokens, terms and the inverted index

From characters to words to a search engine

The computer sees characters, not words

To count or match words, we first have to decide where one word ends and the next begins. That is tokenisation, and it is a design choice:

Don't buy it! The filter (model UKF8001) cost $24.99 at Lowe's, and it leaked after 2-3 weeks...

split() regex \w+ NLTK word_tokenize
Don't Don't Don · t Do · n't
it! it! it it · !
$24.99 $24.99 24 · 99 $ · 24.99
Lowe's, Lowe's, Lowe · s Lowe · 's · ,
2-3 2-3 2 · 3 2-3

No tokeniser is right for everything. For search we want lower-case words and numbers, no punctuation, and contractions (two words shortened into one, like don't = do not) kept whole, so don't stays one token instead of don · t.

Chinese and Japanese don't put spaces between words at all, which makes tokenising them a harder problem.

Tokens and types

How many different words do our reviews use? That number is the size of the vocabulary a search engine has to store.

A token is one occurrence of a word.
A type is a distinct token.
The vocabulary is the set of types.

"the filter and the jug": 5 tokens, 4 types

30,000 reviews tokens types
split() 1,134,947 45,310
lower-case + split() 1,134,947 39,488
our regex tokeniser 1,145,739 17,602

✏️ 1 minute. How many tokens and types in "the filter fits the old fridge but the new filter does not"?

12 tokens, 9 types. the appears 3 times and filter twice: 12 − 2 − 1 = 9.

Zipf's law: a few words are everywhere

rank word count
1 the 62,789
2 i 32,224
3 and 31,474
4 to 31,211
5 a 26,654
…
14 coffee 9,602
  • frequency ∝ 1 / rank: a straight line on log–log axes
  • the top 100 types are 57% of all tokens
  • 42% of the types appear once
  • common words can't tell reviews apart; rare words make a long tail in the index

Normalisation: which tokens count as the same?

Back to our three searches: the exact word leak found 314 reviews, but every form of leak finds 885. Leaks, leaking and leaked are different tokens, and the customer wants all of them.

Step Example Gain Risk
Case folding Filter → filter 45k → 39k types US → us
Stop words drop the, a, of and not half the tokens gone "No leaks" → leaks
Stemming leaks, leaking, leaked → leak 17.6k → 12.0k types generic → gener ← general
Lemmatisation ran → run, mice → mouse real words needs the part of speech

NLTK's English stop-word list has 198 words, and no, not, nor and all 18 n't words are among them. Modern search engines usually keep stop words: "to be or not to be" is made of nothing else.

Stemming by rule: the Porter stemmer (1980)

About 60 rules in 5 steps, with no dictionary. Step 1a, plurals: use the first rule that matches.

Rule Example
sses → ss caresses → caress
ies → i ponies → poni
ss → ss caress → caress
s → (nothing) cats → cat

Step 1b: drop ed or ing, but only if the stem left has a vowel.

plastered → plaster motoring → motor
bled → bled sing → sing

bl and s have no vowel, so they stay.

The stem doesn't have to be a word (poni, replac). It only has to be the same for every form.

What stemming gets wrong, on our reviews

Over-stemming: too much merged

general · generally · generate · generation · generator · generic · generous → gener

Search generic filter and get "generally works fine". Precision ↓

Under-stemming: too little merged

leakage → leakag, leaky → leaki, ran → ran

Search leak and miss leakage. Recall ↓

So why lemmatise? A lemmatiser (WordNet) looks words up in a dictionary instead of chopping endings: ran → run, mice → mouse, and generic stays generic. It never merges unrelated words, but it won't merge leakage with leak either, and it needs the part of speech: as a noun, was → wa.

✏️ On paper, 3 minutes

Apply Porter step 1a (the four rules on the previous slide) to:

(a) glasses   (b) flies   (c) filters   (d) boss   (e) gas

Then: is university, universe → univers over- or under-stemming? What about alumnus, alumni?

(a) glass (b) fli (c) filter (d) boss (e) ga. The rule s → nothing fires on gas too: rules don't know words.

university / universe → univers: over-stemming (different meanings merged). alumnus / alumni staying apart: under-stemming.

Every search so far reads every review, every time

Each search scans all 30,000 reviews, character by character.

  • 100 customers typing a query = 100 full scans of the same, unchanged text
  • The reviews don't change between queries. Can we do the work once?
  • Read every review once, write down which terms it contains, and answer every query from that record

The term–document incidence matrix

D1 D2 D3 D4
filter 1 1 0 0
great 0 1 0 1
ice 0 0 1 0
leak 1 1 1 0
maker 0 0 1 0
price 0 0 0 1
…

D1 Filter leaks after a week.
D2 Great filter. No leaks!
D3 Ice maker leaked water.
D4 Great price, fast delivery.

leak AND NOT ice

1110 AND NOT 0010
= 1110 AND 1101
= 1100 → D1, D2

…and D2 says "No leaks!"

Why nobody stores the matrix

For our reviews:

12,016 terms × 30,000 reviews
= 360 million cells

Only 844,194 of them are 1: 0.23%.

A matrix that is almost all zeros is sparse. Store only the 1s.

Inverted index

filter  →  1 → 2
great   →  2 → 4
ice     →  3
leak    →  1 → 2 → 3

term → its postings list: the sorted doc IDs that contain it. The list's length is the term's document frequency.

AND: merge two postings lists

p1 = 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64  ·  p2 = 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, 55

Compare Do
2 vs 1 2 > 1 move p2 on
2 vs 2 equal keep 2, move both on
4 vs 3 · 4 vs 5 move p2 on · move p1 on
8 vs 5 · 8 vs 8 move p2 on · keep 8
16 vs 13 · 16 vs 21 · 32 vs 21 · 32 vs 34 · 64 vs 34 · 64 vs 55 … p2 runs out: stop

Answer [2, 8] in 12 comparisons. At most len(p1) + len(p2) = 15, because the walk never goes back. Comparing every pair would take 6 × 9 = 54.

✏️ On paper, 3 minutes

leak → 3, 7, 9, 12, 20  ·  ice → 1, 7, 12, 15, 20, 25

  1. leak AND ice: the answer, and the number of comparisons
  2. leak AND NOT ice
  3. leak OR ice: how many documents?
  1. [7, 12, 20], in 7 comparisons: (3,1) (3,7) (7,7)✓ (9,12) (12,12)✓ (20,15) (20,20)✓, and then leak has run out.
  2. [3, 9]
  3. 8 documents: 1, 3, 7, 9, 12, 15, 20, 25 (5 + 6 − 3 shared)

Which list first?

great AND water AND filter AND leak on our reviews. Document frequencies:
filter 8,307 · great 6,531 · water 3,963 · leak 885

Order Candidates left after each step Candidates looked up
as typed: great → water → filter → leak 6,531 → 965 → 597 → 41 8,093
shortest first: leak → water → great → filter 885 → 355 → 74 → 41 1,314

The first number is the first term's own list; each arrow is one more AND. Each candidate is looked up in the next term's list, so the work is the sum of every number except the last: 885 + 355 + 74 = 1,314. We got these counts by running each order on the real index; you can't work them out from the frequencies alone.

Same 41 answers, six times less work. What you can say in advance: an AND never returns more than its shortest list, so starting with leak (885) means no step handles more than 885. The index already stores every term's document frequency, so this plan costs nothing to make.

For (a OR b) AND (c OR d): estimate each OR by the sum of the two frequencies (an upper bound), then start with the smaller OR. That's IIR 1.3, and it's in the practice problems. If someone asks why this doesn't match the merge slide's len(p1) + len(p2): "looked up" assumes each candidate is checked directly in the next list (a set lookup, or skipping ahead in a sorted list). With a plain merge that walks both lists, the long lists' lengths count too, and the two orders cost about 21,000 and 20,000 steps. Shortest first is still never worse, because every intermediate result stays small, but the "six times" is for lookups.

OR, AND NOT, and why there is no plain NOT

Query Walk both lists and … Cost
a OR b keep every ID you pass, plus the leftovers of both len(a) + len(b)
a AND NOT b keep an ID from a when b has passed it without a match len(a) + len(b)
NOT b every document except b's the whole collection

NOT coffee returns about 24,000 reviews. Engines accept NOT only together with a positive term.

Manager's lens: settings that change what customers find

Setting Turn it on and … Ask
Stemming leaking finds leaked; generic finds generally How do people search our catalogue?
Stop words a smaller index; but "not leaking" = "leaking" Are phrases like "The Who" important?
Synonyms fridge finds refrigerator Who maintains the list?
Phrase search "ice maker" ≠ ice … coffee maker Is the index allowed to be bigger?

Every setting moves precision and recall. Decide using real queries from your search logs.

From paper to Python

re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+(?:'[a-z]+)?", text.lower())   # tokenise for search
set(stopwords.words("english"))                      # 198 stop words
PorterStemmer().stem("leaking")                      # 'leak'
WordNetLemmatizer().lemmatize("ran", pos="v")        # 'run'

index = {}
for doc_id, terms in enumerate(doc_terms):
    for t in set(terms):
        index.setdefault(t, []).append(doc_id)       # term -> sorted doc IDs

⚠️ Normalise the query with the same function as the documents, or Leaking will look for a term that isn't in the index.

4:30 · 15 min

Class discussion

Too many results, or none

Query Results
filter 8,307
filter leak 355
filter leak crack 5
filter leak crack warranty 0

Ask: which of the 355 should the manager read first? Boolean search returns a set, not a ranking. Take answers to the four discussion questions in the notebook. On Q4 (scale): the full scan grows with the collection; the index lookup grows with the postings lengths, and the planner keeps those short.

Who can't be found? 🛑

Our tokeniser keeps only a–z and 0–9.

tokenize("पानी लीक हो रहा है") → []   ·   tokenize("café filter") → caf, filter

  1. A customer writes in Hindi, or in Hinglish ("bahut leak ho raha hai"). Does the support team ever see the complaint?
  2. Who notices when a search engine silently drops a group of customers: the vendor, the analyst, or nobody?
  3. Only 30 of our 30,000 reviews (from the US) contain letters our tokeniser throws away. Why is that number no comfort for an Indian support inbox? What would you check first?

Q1: the Hindi review produces no tokens, so it is invisible to every query; the Hinglish one is found by "leak" but not by "leaking" or "leaked". Q2: usually nobody, because missing results don't raise errors; only a recall audit on a sample of real text finds them. Q3: the US reviews say nothing about Indian customers. Check a sample of the real inbox: the share of non-ASCII text, which languages and scripts appear, and whether the tokeniser and stemmer support them (Porter is English-only).

Where Boolean search stops working

355 results, in no order

Rank by how well each review matches → W5 TF-IDF

fridge · refrigerator · freezer

Same meaning, no shared letters → W6 word vectors

"No leaks at all"

The word without the meaning → W4 sentiment

"watr filter"

Typos → edit distance (SLP 2.9) and W3 language models
